notes:
I've written notes for each verse I could find sources on. A few limits up front:

- **Gaps:** I found nothing specific on vv. 33, 35, 36, 38 or 39–40, so those verses are left out (vv. 39–40 appear only in a passing note under v. 44).
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik):** the page cut off around v. 23, so I couldn't use his notes on later verses.
- **Not reached:** I couldn't read D. A. Carson's Gospel Coalition sermon on vv. 27–50 before I ran out of searches and page reads. No bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org pages came up either.
- **Differences between traditions:** none of the pages I read showed Protestant traditions really differing on these verses. Where I could, I've labelled a writer's tradition, but I found no real disputes.
- **Popular modern teaching:** I found nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this passage.

---

**v. 23**
- Guzik says the crowd's voice is not always God's voice. The mob gave no answer to Pilate's "what evil has He done?" and just kept shouting for Jesus' death, by torture through crucifixion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-27/

**v. 24**
- Background: the hand-washing echoes Deuteronomy 21. When a murder went unsolved, the elders would have to offer a sacrifice, and then they would have to wash their hands, declaring, "we are innocent". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-25.html
- Fleming (Bridgeway): Pilate knew Jesus was innocent but didn't want a riot. Fleming holds Pilate guilty for condemning a man he knew was innocent, but says Caiaphas and the others who handed Jesus over were more guilty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-25.html
- On this verse, a "Contending for the Faith" note says the mob's cries do not absolve Pilate of responsibility, but they no doubt help to ease his conscience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-25.html

**v. 25** (the verse with the widest range of views)
- *Ellicott:* the crowd turned the Deuteronomy 21:8 prayer ("Lay not innocent blood to Thy people's charge") into a defiant curse on themselves. He adds that but a fractional part of the people were present, that leaders like Joseph of Arimathea did not agree to it, and that a son does not bear his father's guilt unless he shares in it (Ezekiel 18:20). https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-25.htm
- *Pulpit Commentary:* the leaders stirred the crowd up. It calls the cry a unanimous, a national assumption of guilt, lightly undertaken, terribly vindicated. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-25.htm
- *Gill, Barnes, Clarke:* all see the curse fulfilled in Jerusalem's fall in AD 70. Clarke goes further and says the descendants carry the curse "to this day." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/matthew/27-25.html
- *Matthew Henry:* calls it cruel to bind the curse on unborn children. Yet on some of them, and some of theirs, this blood came, not to condemn them, but to save them, when they repented. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-25.html
- *Calvin (Reformed):* the people took on the curse rashly, as if sure their cause was right. God punished it, yet kept a remnant so that his covenant with Abraham would not be cancelled. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-25.html
- *Desiring God (Baptist):* believers now say "let his blood be on us" not defiantly as the crowds that crucified him, but desperately, depending wholly on his sacrifice. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/let-his-blood-be-on-us
- *LCMS Missouri District (Lutheran):* makes the same ironic point. In faith Christians can pray the words as a sign of our salvation, that we have been washed in the blood of the Lamb. https://mo.lcms.org/may-his-blood-be-on-us/
- *Guzik:* the crowd didn't grasp how wonderful it would be to have Jesus' cleansing blood on them and their children. He also notes that some Christians in antisemitic periods tried to clear Pilate so they could blame the Jews alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-27/
- *Warnings against antisemitism:* the BibleHub study note says the words must not be used to charge the Jewish people as a whole with Christ's death or to excuse hatred against them. It also points out that Gentiles took part too: Pilate, the soldiers and Herod. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-25.htm
- *Greek wording:* a "Contending for the Faith" note, citing R. T. France, says the Greek has no verb. It may be a statement ("His blood IS on us") rather than a wish. The note adds that these are the crowd's words, not a divine prophecy, and that God also heard Jesus' prayer to forgive them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-25.html
- *Church Fathers (early church, shared by Catholic and Orthodox):* BibleHub summarises three. Melito of Sardis saw the verse as irony ending in salvation offered to Israel. Origen stressed God's readiness to forgive. Chrysostom warned believers not to despise Jewish people. These come from a BibleHub summary, not the Fathers' own texts. https://biblehub.com/q/Interpret_His_blood_on_us_in_Christianity.htm

**v. 26**
- Fleming: the flogging was the first step towards crucifixion. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-25.html

**vv. 27–28**
- NET Bible note: the scarlet robe was probably... a military garment which had the color of royal purple, used to mock the charge that Jesus claimed to be a king. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Mat+27%3A28%2C29
- Constable: the Sanhedrin had abused Jesus as a false Messiah; now Pilate's soldiers abused him as a false king. Ironically Jesus was all they charged Him with being. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-29.html
- Matthew Henry: the robe was probably an old red soldier's cloak, mocking the scarlet robes of kings. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-29.html

**v. 29**
- NET Bible note: the thorns unknowingly picture God's curse on humanity (Genesis 3:18) being laid on Jesus. The crown may also parody the "radiant corona" shown on rulers' heads on coins. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Mat+27%3A28%2C29
- Ellicott: picture the whole cohort filing past the "mock-king," kneeling as they passed. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-29.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: these soldiers did in mockery what all nations will one day do in earnest. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-29.htm
- Clarke thinks the crown was meant mainly to make Jesus look ridiculous, not to torture him. Henry disagrees: they could have used straw, but meant it to hurt. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-29.html
- Spurgeon (Baptist): Jesus, mocked and crowned with thorns in our place, shows what sin had brought our race to. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/mocking-the-king/
- D. A. Carson (Reformed): his first "irony of the cross" is that the man who was mocked as king was the King. (Only the search preview, not the full sermon.) https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/sermon/ironies-of-the-cross-matthew-27-27-50/

**v. 30**
- Matthew Henry: the mock sceptre became a real weapon. They probably hit him on the crown of thorns, driving it deeper. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-29.html

**v. 31**
- Matthew Henry: they put his own clothes back on because those would go to the execution squad. No mention is made of removing the crown, so it is commonly (though not certainly) thought that he was crucified wearing it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-29.html

**v. 32**
- Ellicott: "compelled" is the technical word for forced service (as in Matthew 5:41). It implies Jesus was sinking under the load. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-32.htm
- Barnes: John says Jesus carried the cross and Luke says Simon did. There is no contradiction: Jesus carried it first and then probably collapsed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-32.htm
- Mark names Simon's sons, Alexander and Rufus, which suggests Simon became a believer (Pulpit and Meyer). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-32.htm
- Constable: another irony, since Jesus was really bearing Simon's cross by dying in his place. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-32.htm
- Matthew Henry: Jesus first carried the cross as Isaac carried the wood for the burnt-offering. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_027.cfm
- Bengel quotes Athanasius: a mere man carried the cross so all would know the Lord died not his own death but ours. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-32.htm
- Church Fathers, via a BibleHub summary: Chrysostom saw in Simon the Gentiles' first share in the Passion. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_Simon_carry_Jesus_cross.htm
- Many Fathers thought Simon was a pagan, picturing the conversion of the nations. One sermon notes this view can't be ruled out. https://biblehub.com/sermons/matthew/27-32.htm

**v. 34**
- Ellicott: refusing to drink shows Jesus' resolve to drink his Father's cup to the last drop, without dulling the pain or his communion with the Father. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-34.htm
- Barnes: "gall" can mean anything very bitter. The drink was given to dull the senses; He was unwilling to blunt the pains of dying. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-34.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary and Wesley disagree on the motive:
  - *Pulpit:* it was not an additional insult... but a usual act of kindliness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-34.html
  - *John Wesley (Methodist):* it was given "out of derision." He suggests Matthew's "gall" is the myrrh in Mark's account, called gall for its bitterness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-34.html
- Constable: Matthew wrote "gall" to make the fulfilment of Psalm 69:21 clearer. Jesus chose to endure the cross fully conscious. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/27-34.html
- Gill: Jesus tasted it to show he did not despise their offer, but refused anything that would prolong his life or cloud his mind. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/ncv/matthew/27-34.html

**v. 37**
- Matthew Henry (Concise): it was usual to shame criminals with a notice of their crime, so one was set over Christ's head. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-43.htm

**v. 42**
- Barnes: "He saved others" was probably cutting irony, not an admission. Jesus didn't come down because the time for atonement had come, and those who ignored his other miracles wouldn't have believed anyway. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-43.htm

**v. 43**
- Ellicott: it seems amazing that priests quoted Psalm 22:8 word for word. But they didn't treat the psalm as Messianic, and its wording came naturally to their lips. https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-43.htm
- The Cambridge note on that page: The chief priests unconsciously apply to the true Messiah the very words of a Messianic psalm. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-43.htm
- BibleHub study note: the taunt echoes Satan's "If You are the Son of God" in the wilderness temptation (Matthew 4:6). https://biblehub.com/matthew/27-43.htm
- Pulpit Commentary notes striking parallels with Wisdom 2:13–20, about the persecuted righteous man called God's son. (Wisdom is in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.) It puts this down to the "typical nature" of Christ's treatment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-43.htm
- Older critical commentaries:
  - *Meyer* notes the Jews declared Psalm 22 non-Messianic.
  - *Expositor's Greek Testament* doubts the line was really spoken by the Sanhedrin, suggesting it reads like an echo of the psalm.
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/27-43.htm

**v. 44**
- Matthew records three rounds of mockery: passers-by (vv. 39–40), the religious leaders (vv. 41–43) and the crucified criminals (v. 44). https://biblehub.com/q/Implication_of_Jesus_trust_in_God.htm
